skyline.text: Amit Varma’s cut lip becomes a metaphor for India’s pensions
Ajay Shah on the put option hidden in the UPS
In 1889, a pension from age 70 cost almost nothing

footnote.text: Everything that the government does has a cost.

brief.head: Past 60, more to go
brief.text: Life expectancy at birth in India is about 74, Ajay Shah said, but those who reach 60 or 70 can expect more years still. {065-C04}

brief.head: The test of a state
brief.text: Like winning a war, getting pensions right is a raw test of whether a state can think, Shah said: it needs calculations over a hundred years. {065-C05}

brief.head: Send it abroad
brief.text: Shah’s one regret about the NPS: it should have been globally diversified from day one, with perhaps 60 to 80 per cent invested abroad. {065-C12}

brief.head: Show your workings
brief.text: The UPS came with no calculations, Shah said. For OROP, he and Renuka Sane published all their code and assumptions so anyone could rerun the numbers. {065-C16}

brief.head: With eyes open
brief.text: The NPS took nothing from existing staff, Shah said. Only new recruits joined, warned in the job advertisement: if you don’t like it, don’t join the government. {065-C10}

thought.text: A country can only be as good as its intellectuals.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, explaining why reforms decay when the thinking class walks away

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on India’s pension promises
lead.head: A wound that will not clot
body: Amit Varma arrived at the shoot with a shaving cut that would not stop bleeding. With Ajay Shah’s blessing he aimed a hairdryer at his lip, and by the time the cameras rolled he had a metaphor.
A shallow cut heals on its own. A body with a thousand deep cuts and no way to clot keeps bleeding. That, Varma said, made a pretty apt metaphor for the episode’s subject: India’s pensions.

Varma first heard of the danger in mid-2023 from the politician Jayaprakash Narayan, who told him it kept him up at night. {065-S02} Varma had never heard of the NPS or the OPS. “No, Amit,” Narayan replied, “we are destroying our future generation.”

That led him to Shah, one of the architects of the New Pension Scheme. This episode was prompted by its successor, the Unified Pension Scheme, which, Varma said, does things to the NPS that make it just like the OPS.
An economist both hosts respect, Varma added, has warned that it could lead to the greatest fiscal disaster India has seen.
## Promises that grow

Shah’s case rests on one distinction. A defined-benefit pension guarantees a payout for life, paid in effect by the young to the old. A defined-contribution pension makes you save into an account that is yours alone.
“Every single defined benefit program in the world has got into trouble,” Shah said. {065-C02}

India’s old scheme gave civil servants a 50 per cent defined-benefit pension. When Gautam Bhardwaj and Surendra Dave put a present value on those promises, the answer was 68 per cent of GDP. {065-C06}
## A bipartisan rescue

The NDA’s big four, Yashwant Sinha, Jaswant Singh, Advani and Vajpayee, grasped it at once. Vajpayee signed the file in December 2002, and from January 2004 new central government recruits joined the NPS instead.
What struck Varma was what came next. The UPA government that followed re-examined the reform from scratch and kept it. Manmohan Singh and Chidambaram, he said, got it too.
When the CPI(M) would not back a law, Chidambaram ran the scheme for nine years on private contracts that bound fund managers to inspection and disclosure. The law came only in 2013.
## How it came undone
Then, Shah said, the community of thinkers that had made the case for the NPS went home. Flaws went unfixed, and nobody redid the calculation of implicit pension debt.

Young civil servants who had joined the NPS with their eyes open began demanding the old scheme. The Congress, Varma noted, pushed it in state after state, though Shah had once briefed Rahul Gandhi on pension reform.
Varma could not understand why a small group carried such weight when the cost falls on everyone. Politicians “who should know better, who do know better, are actually pandering to them”, he said.
The UPS, Shah said, tops up any annuity below 50 per cent from a guarantee fund: in derivatives terms a put option, whose cost nobody has published. {065-C15}

His broader lesson was about reform itself. The NPS was structural: your money in your account, nothing for politicians to fiddle with. Parametric reforms leave the old machine and its dials in place. {065-C17}
Varma turned the idea on himself. A weekend locked away to write, or an occasional sprint, is a parametric fix; daily habits are structural.
“We talk here about reforming the state,” he said. “I tell the reader, reform thyself.”

second.label: The 2004 handover
second.head: Saved by a market crash
second.deck: How a stock market panic in May 2004 helped keep pension reform alive
body: In the 2004 campaign, a Congress candidate in Delhi tried to stir anger over lost defined-benefit pensions. It got no traction, Ajay Shah said.

Then, on 17 May 2004, the stock market crashed after some CPM politicians talked of tearing the house down. Shah makes a causal claim: the crisis helped Sonia Gandhi settle on Manmohan Singh, Chidambaram, Montek Ahluwalia and C Rangarajan as her economic team. {065-S07}

These were, Shah said, the people who had been leading the reforms all along, and the market quickly lost its jitters. The new UPA government re-examined the NPS from scratch. Shah spent half a day walking Rahul Gandhi and young Congress MPs through it, at a session organised by Bibek Debroy. {065-S08}

quote.text: This is the dream team of the people that had been leading the reforms all along.

second.caption: the 2004 market crash

third.head: Twice the bill till 2029
body: For about a generation, Ajay Shah said, governments pay twice: the pensions of those already retired, and the 10 per cent higher salaries that fund the new accounts. {065-C11}

“And this was done by design that there will be a transition generation where you will pay twice,” he said. The payoff was due around 2029, when payments to the older generation would start subsiding.

With no researchers modelling the transition, politicians saw only the extra cost, and some lost their nerve just before the payoff. On one side, Shah said, were some one lakh, two lakh organised young civil servants; on the other, no public discourse at all. {#lakh}
Amit Varma added that the 25-year wait applies to state finances: individuals in a well-run NPS would do much better than under the OPS.
third.caption: the generation that pays twice

p2.title: Promises, promises
p2.deck: How pensions grew from a kindness into a menace, how India fixed them, and how the fix is fraying

sections.label: How it began
sections.head: From whip-round to time bomb
sections.caption: how pensions became a bloody mess
body: Pensions began as small acts of grace. At one port, Ajay Shah recalled, when workers’ health broke from lugging cartons, the current workers would pool a little bit of money to give them a pension. {#port}

Because people died quickly, the gesture cost little. Bismarck, then the leader of Germany, turned it into an affair of state. In 1889 he announced a pension of 50 per cent of the last year’s income, paid from age 70, at a time when there were no antibiotics and doctors still used leeches.
“So once again, this was a tiny gesture which feels nice but was not economically material,” Shah said. {065-S03}
## Three forces

Over the following century the same idea became, in Shah’s words, a bloody mess. People lived longer, so lifelong payments were worth more. Birth rates collapsed, so fewer young people paid for more old ones. And democratic politics kept chipping away at the terms: the percentage and the starting age.

Here Shah called himself a one-handed economist. Every defined-benefit programme in the world, he said, has reneged on its promises, or will. {065-C02} Amit Varma explained the phrase: the US President Harry Truman wanted an economist who would not keep saying “on the other hand”.

~ Varma added that these dangers are easy to see with a thirty- or forty-year view. But politicians’ horizons are short, and in India there is always an election around the corner in some state or other.

quote.text: There is not one defined benefit program that has stayed out of trouble.

sections.label: Chalk and cheese
sections.head: Three rooms that look alike
sections.caption: nominal, inflation- and wage-indexed pensions
body: Ajay Shah began with terms. A nominal pension pays a fixed sum, say Rs 50 on a wage of Rs 100, for the rest of your life. With wise financial planning it can be achieved.

Index it to inflation and the cost roughly doubles, Shah said. Index it to the wages of today’s workers and it becomes astronomically expensive. “There does not exist a wise management strategy through which wage indexation can be obtained,” he said. {065-C03}

They sound alike, he warned, but they are chalk and cheese. The fair-sounding demand behind one rank, one pension, that a general retired twenty years ago should get what a new one gets, blows up the numbers.
## Yours, not ours

Against all of this Shah set the defined-contribution pension. The state uses its power only to make you save into your own account. Nobody pays for anyone else, and nobody else can get their claws on your money. {065-C01}
Defined benefits, he said, pit the young against the old: every Marxist dream of class warfare.

~ Amit Varma put it in terms of a company. An employer that overpromises pensions goes out of business. The state, spending other people’s money on other people, as in Milton Friedman’s matrix, faces no such check.

quote.text: The beauty of a defined contribution approach is there is no socialisation, which is the root of all evil.

sections.label: The old scheme
sections.head: Sixty-eight per cent of GDP
sections.caption: the 68 per cent bombshell
body: The Old Pension Scheme paid civil servants a 50 per cent defined-benefit pension. Civil servants are a tiny fraction of Indians, and for years nobody noticed. Then payouts in the railways, the military and the civil service began to surge, and by the 1990s, Ajay Shah said, simple extrapolations showed the country could not afford them.

In 1998, under the Vajpayee government, Anand Bordia, a joint secretary in Maneka Gandhi’s Ministry of Social Justice, worked with Gautam Bhardwaj to set up Project Oasis. It was led by Surendra Dave, founding chairman of SEBI. Shah sat on its expert committee.
Dave’s intuition was that equity returns, modern technology and index funds bought by auction could make a cheap, attractive pension system.
## The stock, not the flow

Bhardwaj and Dave then put a present value on the promises made to civil servants: 68 per cent of GDP. {065-S04} Until then people had watched the flow of payments, doubling every six years, without seeing the stock. {065-C06}
The number reached Yashwant Sinha, Jaswant Singh, Advani and Vajpayee, the big four of the NDA cabinet, and all of them got it.
~ Shah drew a line to defence. A mighty military is made out of economics, he said, and the first item on the agenda of military reform is to solve the pensions mess. {#military}

quote.text: That was an eye opener and it helped wake up everybody on the scale of this problem.

sections.label: The new scheme
sections.head: Bought, not sold
sections.caption: how the NPS was designed
body: The NPS, Ajay Shah said, asks the state to make a civil servant do what a sophisticated saver would do anyway: save, hold equities, use index funds and keep fees low. {065-C07}

Twenty per cent of pay went into a personal account. The money was run by a small pool of fund managers, six in the original intent, chosen by public tender and running index funds. The only test of an index fund, Shah said, is how little it charges.
Index funds were politically safe too: nobody could demand a CBI investigation into why a fund manager did badly.
## No salesmen

Shah called one saying in finance deeply toxic: that fund management is sold, not bought. {065-C08} It is the world of Shah Rukh Khan in the advertisements, crazy commissions and a million agents nudging friends and family into tax-saving products.

The NPS was to be bought. Fund managers would get bulk money without even knowing their customers’ names. An expert committee would set the default mix of equities, corporate bonds and government bonds, and anyone could override it online.
~ And every month, Shah said, members get an SMS telling them what they now own, a number that remorselessly goes up. {#sms}

quote.text: There’s a phrase in finance which is a deeply toxic one which says that fund management is sold, not bought.

sections.label: What went wrong
sections.head: The reformers went home
sections.caption: the pension community that disbanded
body: From 1998 to 2004, Ajay Shah said, India had a real pension reform community: research papers, seminars, op-eds, an intellectual ferment. Then the decisions were taken, everyone thought the job was done, and the community disbanded. {065-S12}
“And without the ecosystem, you’re nothing,” Shah said.

Small flaws in the NPS went unfixed. Equity exposure stayed timid, a failure of nerve by the civil servants in charge. Military pensions drifted into OROP. Pension work moved from KP Krishnan’s DEA to the DFS, and institutional memory went with it.
## Who pays, who shouts

When young civil servants began demanding the OPS, there was nobody left to argue back. Karnataka once informally asked Shah to spend a day with its trade unions; he did, and calls it a matter of talking, engaging and showing calculations. {#karnataka}

States that go back to the OPS cannot touch the NPS money, which is the workers’ private property. Last he heard, Shah said drily, it was not yet easy for Indian governments to expropriate it. {065-J13}
~ Amit Varma drew the moral: passing a policy is not the end of the story. Quoting what he called Jefferson’s alleged phrase, he said eternal vigilance is still required. {065-J15}

quote.text: Now, in hindsight, the biggest tragedy was that that community disbanded.

sections.label: The new storm
sections.head: A guarantee nobody priced
sections.caption: the Unified Pension Scheme and its put option
body: A storm broke over the outdoor shoot. When the hosts returned, Amit Varma said the UPS was one of those storms that would not pass easily.

The Unified Pension Scheme keeps a fund, Ajay Shah said, but promises that if a retiree’s annuity falls below 50 per cent, a guarantee fund will fill the gap. In the language of derivatives, that is a put option on the portfolio, and put options can be pretty expensive. {065-C15}

Nobody has published the calculations. Pension promises can run to 50 or 100 per cent of GDP, Shah said; in the United States the implicit pension debt is 200 per cent. {#usdebt} Without the numbers, the guarantee could become a contingent liability dangling over the Indian state.
## No dials to twiddle

The NPS mattered, Shah argued, because it was a structural reform: your own money in your own account, with no fudge factors. Parametric reforms keep the old machine and leave dials for politics to twiddle. {065-C17}
NREGS, he said, was promised to be self-liquidating: as incomes rose, nobody would want to work for 100 rupees a day. {#nregs} Instead its daily payment kept going up.

~ He feared the same creep in any government-run universal healthcare system, and borrowed a line from Bruce Springsteen for India’s missing thinkers: “Well man, the poets around here don’t write nothing at all.” {065-J17}

quote.text: In parametric reforms, we hold a basic edifice intact and twiddle with some dials.

side.boxText: The Project Oasis report of 2000, from an expert committee led by Surendra Dave, set out the design that became the NPS: personal accounts, equities and index funds bought at auction for razor-thin fees. Ajay Shah sat on the committee. {065-R01}

contQuote.text: The point, however, is to change the Overton window, is to legitimize the complex reforms that are needed in the country that are beyond the horizon of an average policymaker.

p3.title: Inside the room
p3.deck: Cabinet meetings, insurance chiefs, a bleeding lip and a minister’s candour

stories.caption: the decisive cabinet meeting
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how the NDA cabinet signed up for reform
stories.head: Eyes closed, mind made up
body: Ajay Shah worked directly with Yashwant Sinha, S Narayan and UK Sinha, and describes a younger, less polite version of himself talking fire and brimstone about what would happen if India did not fix the problem.

They carried the case up to Jaswant Singh, Advani and Vajpayee. Shah, then in the Ministry of Finance, recalls the prime minister sending back variation after variation: suppose you do it like this, show me the calculations. {065-S05}

Vajpayee finally settled on what Shah calls “ten, ten and ninety”: a 10 per cent wage hike, so that 100 became 110, and a deduction of 20 into a personal pension account, leaving 90. It was, Shah said, pure political judgement of what was fair.
Shah was not in the decisive cabinet meeting. UK Sinha was, and told him the story. The big four favoured the reform; many other ministers did not.

Vajpayee, Shah said, “had a way of either appearing to be asleep or actually being asleep in meetings”. {065-J09} That day he sat with his eyes almost closed, taking in the debate. At the end he ruled: “Yeh to karna hi hai.” This simply has to be done. {065-S06}
He signed the file on 12 December 2002. {#signature} From 1 January 2004, every new central government employee went into the new system.
~ Shah offers Vajpayee’s line as a slogan for every dreamer, every reformer, every do-gooder: you have to bite the bullet, and you have to do these things.
stories.why: A reform that pays off over decades needs a leader willing to spend political capital on gains no voter today will see. Vajpayee asked for the numbers, judged what was fair, and then decided.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma pictured a web-series scene of Vajpayee gazing at a young Shah. Shah deflated it: he never sat with Vajpayee on this question. {065-J08}

stories.start: And the other was that there was a rebellion by the insurance companies
stories.end: later in the day we were informed, boss has decided we're doing NPS
stories.caption: the fourteen insurance CEOs
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the day the insurance lobby lost
stories.head: Fourteen chiefs, one reply
body: The insurance industry wanted pensions for itself. “We don’t want no stinking pension fund managers, we don’t want no stinking index funds,” was how Ajay Shah put its case. {065-J10}

Chidambaram called a meeting with fourteen insurance CEOs, Surendra Dave beside him. Shah could attend but must not speak. Each CEO said they knew the business, could do index funds and could even offer guarantees.

Then Chidambaram turned to Dave. What followed, Shah said, was the most masterly fifteen-minute rebuttal, while his own heart was in his mouth. Nobody said anything after it. {065-S09} Later that day word came: the boss has decided, we’re doing NPS.
~ Why it mattered, Shah said: until retirement a pension is just fund management, your money, inherited by your heirs. Insurance belongs only at the end, when savings become an annuity. {065-C09}

quote.text: But Dave’s response was absolutely masterly, and nobody said anything.

stories.start: So I woke up in the morning, as one tends to do
stories.end: episode today, you know, I feel that that's a pretty apt metaphor
stories.caption: the bleeding lip
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s morning before the shoot
stories.head: The bleeding lip libertarian
body: Amit Varma shaved on the morning of the shoot, making “some minimal effort” to look presentable. {065-J01} His mind wandered, and he cut his lip.

The cut kept bleeding. Varma would not cancel: “I don’t care if I die, but we gotta shoot.” {065-J02} Ajay Shah, wearing his scientific hat, said oxygen makes blood clot and told him to stand in front of a fan. Varma asked if a hairdryer would do, and became perhaps the first person in history to aim one at his lips.
His serious thought: a shallow cut stops bleeding, but a body with a thousand deep cuts and no clotting bleeds on and on. He found it an apt metaphor for the episode’s subject. {065-S01}
~ The other was a label: this nation is regrettably too full of bleeding-heart liberals, and here was a bleeding lip libertarian. {065-J03}

quote.text: But imagine a body where you have a thousand deep cuts and the mechanism of clotting isn’t there

stories.start: when I first began discussing inflation targeting with Yashwan Sena in 2002 and 2003
stories.end: But in 2002 and 2003, we were not ready for that
stories.caption: the finance minister’s advice
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a lesson from Yashwant Sinha
stories.head: A mere finance minister
body: In 2002 and 2003, Ajay Shah tried to sell inflation targeting to the finance minister, Yashwant Sinha. Sinha said the idea was way too far from conventional Indian intellectual discourse.
“Your baradari is not ready for this,” Sinha told him. India’s economists, he said, did not understand monetary economics, and the larger community would have to shift its position first.
Then came the line. “Then who am I? I’m a mere finance minister. I can only follow. I can’t lead.” {065-S11} Inflation targeting did arrive, in 2015.
~ For Shah the moral is a theory of change: whispering in a joint secretary’s ear only produces small changes within what officials already accept. The task is to change the Overton window. {065-C14}
stories.why: Even powerful ministers act within the range of ideas their experts accept. Lasting reform, Shah argued, needs a broad community that changes what is thinkable. Amit Varma counted the years: thirteen, the long road to change. {065-R15}

quiz.q: When Bismarck announced his pension in 1889, from what age was it paid, and why was it cheap?
quiz.a: From seventy; with no antibiotics, few people lived much beyond that age.

quiz.q: What did Gautam Bhardwaj and Surendra Dave find the civil service pension promises were worth?
quiz.a: 68 per cent of GDP, for a tiny sliver of the population.

quiz.q: Under Vajpayee’s “ten, ten and ninety”, what happened to a civil servant’s pay of 100?
quiz.a: It rose to 110; 20 went into a pension account, leaving 90.

quiz.q: What did Vajpayee say at the end of the decisive cabinet meeting on pensions?
quiz.a: “Yeh to karna hi hai”: this simply has to be done.

quiz.q: Who answered the fourteen insurance CEOs in Chidambaram’s meeting, and how long did he take?
quiz.a: Surendra Dave, with what Ajay Shah calls a masterly fifteen-minute rebuttal.

quiz.q: In the language of derivatives, what is the UPS promise to top up annuities?
quiz.a: A put option on the portfolio, and put options can be pretty expensive.
